startup.name: Nine Fives
startup.one_liner: RF test equipment for next-gen spacecraft, drones, and cellphones
startup.description: Nine Fives builds modern radio frequency test equipment and AI-ready test automation to challenge incumbents in a test and measurement market of roughly $5B in RF equipment (the founders cite $130B for all test equipment). Paying customers are hardware teams in aerospace, drones and telecom who buy instruments and want faster bring-up. A three person team in San Francisco, Spring 2026 batch.

yc_acceptance.basis: Blind test: the company is known to have been accepted, so this is a placeholder note and not an estimate. For reference the prior for a random applicant is about 1 percent (references/yc_acceptance.md) and a three person hard tech team targeting a large incumbent market would sit near the upper end of that range.
yc_acceptance.why_it_fails: Not applicable in this test because the company was accepted. If YC had said no, the likely reasons would be unproven founder credentials in RF engineering, no shipped instrument yet, and a capital intensive hardware plan that competes head on with Keysight and Rohde and Schwarz, with no named customer to show demand.

anchors.source: python3 -I scripts/base_rates.py --years 2022-2025 --industry Industrials --calibration-only gave seed 67% (n=12, CI 39-86%, median 3 months to seed); the 2018-2022 Industrials cohort gave 69% (n=13). The test defines seed as a round above $500K within about 12 months, so the anchor is trimmed.
anchors.adjustment_reason: Slightly below the 67% anchor (ratio 0.87) because the test requires the round within 12 months and a three person hardware team has no revenue yet. Hard tech and aerospace tags are currently favored by investors, which stops a deeper cut.

bands.rationale: Small pre seed or seed from hard tech funds, near the 2022+ median seed raise of $2.6M for Industrials.
Typical seed led by a defense or hard tech seed fund on the strength of a spacecraft or drone design partner.
Upside band if a marquee aerospace customer or a pivot to defense test systems appears.
Thin round of angels and a small fund with a SAFE close to the YC cap.

ladder.why_it_fails: The most likely stop is that three founders with no revenue cannot show a working instrument that beats a refurbished Keysight unit within a year. Investors fund hardware test tools slowly, buyers are conservative and procure through long cycles, and Ohm (W23) took months and a pivot toward software to find a seed. A seed above $500K needs a named design partner, and if the first prototype slips past the demo day window the round slips with it.

anchors.source: python3 -I scripts/base_rates.py --years 2018-2022 --industry Industrials --calibration-only gave series_a 31% unconditional and 44% given seed (n=9); B2B 2018-2022 gave 31% given seed (n=74).
anchors.adjustment_reason: Near the anchors. The 2018-2022 Industrials row is small (n=13) so the 0.75 times floor from the backtest is respected. Slow instrument sales and long qualification cycles hold it just under the conditional anchor.

bands.rationale: Hardware Series A at the low end of the 2022+ median of about $15M.
Standard Series A with defense or aerospace revenue and repeat orders.
Upside if drones or space customers drive fast unit growth.
Thin or bridge style A with a flat or down valuation after slow sales.

ladder.why_it_fails: Series A fails if instruments sell as one off pilots instead of repeat purchases and gross margin stays low because of component cost and manufacturing. Corvus Robotics (S18) needed four years of hardware iteration before it announced larger rounds, and test equipment buyers rarely commit until a product has years of calibration history. Without about $1M of recurring revenue, Series A investors will treat this as a services shop.

anchors.source: python3 -I scripts/base_rates.py --years 2018-2022 --industry B2B --calibration-only gave series_b 35% given series_a (n=23); Industrials 2018-2022 gave 50% (n=4, anecdote).
anchors.adjustment_reason: Slightly below the anchors because hardware scale up needs manufacturing capital, but within 0.75 times of them.

bands.rationale: Modest B for a profitable niche instrument maker.
Median 2022+ Series B of about $37M to $40M with an enterprise and defense customer base.
Upside if the platform becomes a standard in drone or satellite production test.
Down or flat round from slower growth and weaker hardware margins than planned.

ladder.why_it_fails: Series B fails when the company cannot turn a handful of aerospace customers into a repeatable sales motion, and when a large incumbent matches the AI automation features. Hardware companies hit gross margin and working capital limits, so growth is capped unless supply chain control (the company's stated edge) really lowers cost. Analogs show many hardware peers stall between A and B on inventory financing.

anchors.source: knowledge/.../stage_benchmarks.md conditional rate for series C given B is 36% (n=55); B2B 2018-2022 gave series_c 50% given B (n=8).
anchors.adjustment_reason: At the anchor, since survivors to B are a selected group, though instruments rarely grow fast enough to need a large C.

bands.rationale: Typical 2022+ Series C with a median near $45M to $74M.
Growth round on strong defense and space demand.
Upside if it becomes a category leader in RF test.
Smaller structured round or a strategic investment from an incumbent or defense prime.

ladder.why_it_fails: Series C fails when growth plateaus at a niche instrument business of tens of millions in revenue, which is a good company but not a venture scale one. Incumbents can acquire the company before a large round, and the next step usually becomes an acquisition by Keysight, Rohde and Schwarz or a defense prime instead.

outcomes.why_it_fails: The most likely failure is a slow commercial ramp in a conservative market, where engineers keep buying trusted instruments and the three person team runs out of money before a product earns calibration credibility. The Industrials cohort shows 31% of 2018-2022 companies shut down, and hardware companies fail more slowly and more quietly than software.

killers.risk: Incumbents (Keysight, Rohde and Schwarz) and trusted refurbished units win on calibration, support and procurement habit
killers.evidence: The top five vendors held about 47% of RF test equipment in 2025 and Keysight alone about 30%, so buyers have strong default choices.
killers.mitigation: Pick one narrow instrument for drones or small satellites where incumbents are overpriced and sell it to design partners first.

killers.risk: Hardware capital intensity and supply chain slow growth and cap margins
killers.evidence: Instruments need components, calibration and inventory, which makes cash conversion slow for a seed stage team of three.
killers.mitigation: Pre sell units, use contract manufacturers and keep first products low parts count.

killers.risk: Founders lack the RF depth and credibility to sell to aerospace engineers
killers.evidence: Team size is three and the description gives no named customers or prior RF product history, so credibility is unproven as of the batch start.
killers.mitigation: Recruit a senior RF advisor and publish measured specifications against incumbent gear.

killers.risk: AI test automation is built into incumbent software or by software first rivals
killers.evidence: Daqstra style software layers and incumbent software suites can automate test benches without new hardware.
killers.mitigation: Make the hardware and software integration the product, not the automation alone.

competition_now.traction: Broad installed base across telecom and aerospace.

technical_complexity.rationale: RF front ends, calibration accuracy and firmware are hard but a small expert team can ship one narrow instrument in months. Matching incumbent specifications across a full range is not feasible for three people, so the plan has to be narrow.

takeover_risk.rationale: Incumbents have distribution and could copy features, but they move slowly and price high, and a cheap modular instrument for drones is not their priority. A well funded copy would take about two years.

evidence.claim: The RF test equipment market is estimated at about $5.3B in 2025, growing to about $9B by 2035.
Market reports forecast steady growth near 6% a year driven by 5G, satellites and drones.

narrative.headline: A narrow, credible RF instrument could reach seed, but it must beat entrenched incumbents.
narrative.general_summary: Nine Fives is a three person hardware team aiming at the RF test market, which is large and steady but controlled by Keysight, Rohde and Schwarz and a few others. Industrials companies in recent cohorts reach seed quickly, with a median of three months, but only a minority reach Series A and the sample is small. Hardware sales cycles are long and margins depend on supply chain control, so a seed above $500K within a year is likely while later rounds are less certain. Slow and profitable paths are common for companies with paying customers, and a pivot to software or defense test systems is a plausible upside.

assumptions: Blind test using only the batch start description; no founder backgrounds are known.
Industrials cohort base rates are small (n=12 to 13) and treated as anecdotes; B2B cohorts were used to widen.
Seed means a round above $500K within about 12 months of the batch start.
Coverage per knowledge/coverage.md: 662 of 6,399 companies researched.
